title: KV Cache Architecture — eviction, memory pools, fragmentation (draft)
content:
Overview:
This draft captures the KV cache architecture decisions we need for the serving runtime: physical layout, memory pools and allocators, eviction policies, and fragmentation mitigation. The intent is to provide a design that meets our production goals: low latency tail, predictable memory usage, and graceful degradation under load.

Goals / constraints:
- Per-model and per-shard KV cache to reduce cross-tenant interference.
- Tight tail-latency SLO (p99 generation token latency) — cache ops must be bounded
- Minimal stopping-the-world compaction; avoid global locks that block inference threads
- Support variable KV item sizes (kv entries are attention KV blocks across layers).
- Operate across GPU (device memory) and host pinned pools with transparent migration.

High-level layout:
- Namespace: cache_key = (model_id, variant, layer_idx, seq_prefix_hash)
- Index: a small in-memory hash table (per-shard) mapping cache_key -> entry descriptor (fixed-size). Descriptor contains: location pointer, size, timestamp, refcount token. Descriptors live in host memory for quick lookup.
- Storage: actual KV payload lives in memory pools (device / host). Pools are composed of fixed-size slabs (see allocator section).

Memory pools & allocator strategy:
- Two-tier allocator: slab allocator for common KV sizes and fallback large-object pool.
- Slab classes: predefine size classes (e.g., 1KB, 2KB, 4KB, 8KB, 16KB, 32KB, 64KB). Most KV blocks cluster — we will collect telemetry to refine classes.
- Slab implementation: per-shard, per-device free lists to avoid global contention. Each slab is a contiguous chunk (prefetch-friendly) with header metadata kept separate to avoid racing on payload writes.
- Large-object pool: allocate via buddy allocator / page allocator for entries larger than max slab size. Track large allocations in a separate LRU queue.
- Device vs host pools: prefer device memory for hot entries. Eviction can migrate cold entries from device -> host to free device GPU RAM. Migration is done asynchronously and counts as a demotion operation.

Allocation lifecycle:
1) Lookup descriptor. If hit and refcount > 0: touch timestamp, return pointer.
2) Miss path: reserve slab slot from per-shard allocator (fast-path). If no slab available, try steal from local free lists; then try global scavenger; then allocate large object; if all fail, trigger evictions (see policy).
3) During allocation the descriptor is updated under a fine-grained lock. Once payload is written, refcount is incremented atomically and made visible.

Eviction policy:
- Multi-tier eviction: soft limit and hard limit per-shard + global budget.
- Soft limit triggers background eviction (low-priority thread) to bring usage under soft threshold. Hard limit triggers synchronous eviction on allocation paths.
- Policy: combined LFU/LRU (windowed LRU with frequency boost). We maintain a small in-memory approximate LFU sketch per shard (count-min or TinyLFU) plus an LRU ring for recently used items. The eviction rank = frequency_boost * freq + recency_score. Frequency gives preference to long-lived hot prefixes; recency keeps recent accesses.
- Pinning: certain entries (e.g., KV for currently running generation requests) are pinned via refcount and excluded from eviction. Administrative pins (operator) supported.
- Demotion: first attempt to demote device entries to host (if host memory free). Demotion is cheaper than full eviction because it preserves payload. If insufficient host memory, proceed to full eviction.
- Batch eviction: eviction picks batch sizes tuned to avoid many small deallocations; this improves throughput and reduces fragmentation risk.

Fragmentation & compaction strategies:
- Slab allocator reduces internal fragmentation for common sizes.
- External fragmentation (from many differently-sized large objects) handled by: 1) buddy allocator support for coalescing free pages; 2) periodic light-weight compaction for device memory where contiguous chunks can be consolidated. Compaction should be incremental and off the hot path.
- Defragmentation windows: schedule during low-load windows and adaptive trigger when free contiguous runs fall below threshold.
- Metadata-only fast-scan: maintain coarse-grained free-run histograms per pool to decide whether compaction is worth running.

Concurrency & safety:
- Fine-grained locking: per-descriptor and per-slab locks. Reads use lock-free descriptor reads + atomic refcount increment. Writes/evictions take slab-level locks only.
- Eviction isolation: eviction scans will skip pinned/refcounted entries; if eviction fails to free enough space, allocation will fail fast and bubble up a capacity error (caller can fallback to smaller context or alternative model).

Instrumentation & metrics:
- Per-shard metrics: total_bytes, used_bytes, device_bytes, host_bytes, allocations/s, evictions/s, demotions/s, compactions/s, avg_alloc_latency, p99_alloc_latency, fragmentation_ratio (free_frag_bytes / total_free_bytes).
- Telemetry feeds to Optimize: heatmaps of size distribution, lifetime histograms, hot-key lists for model owners.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Unit tests for allocator behaviors, simulated workloads (small/big KV mixes), and race conditions.
- Chaos tests: forced OOM on device pool, forced demotion failures, and stress generation with long-sequence generation.
- Canary rollout: start with non-critical models, monitor p99 latency and evictions; progressive ramp.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact slab size classes: collect production telemetry to finalize.
- Frequency sketch parameters (window size, decay rate).
- Migration cost model: should we proactively demote based on access rates? Design a cost function.
- GPU pinned memory vs pageable: interaction with CUDA allocation and fragmentation patterns needs benchmarking.
- Integration with routing policies: preference for routing long-context requests to nodes with warmed KV.

References:
- Related docs: kv-cache-architecture-spec-v2 (see previous revisions), serving-runtime/kv-cache-ops.md (TODO), JIRA-RT-4567 for follow-up implementation tickets.
